title: A Interior for the Postcards
premise: Tamsin Eastwick, once a celebrated composition prodigy who abandoned music after a scandal involving her late mother's unpublished work, returns to the Ashcombe Conservatory as a janitor to stay close to the building where her mother taught and to remain invisible. When a radio broadcast airs a song her mother wrote but never recorded—credited to a stranger named Vivian Marsh—Tamsin realizes someone is systematically claiming her mother's catalog. As she investigates, she uncovers that the 'stranger in the old photographs' is a woman her mother loved and betrayed, and that Tamsin's own silence years ago enabled the theft. The novel ends with Tamsin testifying before a small arbitration panel not for legal victory but for public truth, then finally playing her mother's unfinished final piece at the conservatory, choosing belonging over anonymity.
about_author: Coral Halloran is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the unclaimed compositions of forgotten women composers. She writes literary fiction about inheritance, music, and the quiet violence of being erased.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She begins her first week as a janitor at Ashcombe Conservatory, mopping floors beneath practice rooms where students play pieces she once could have written. She keeps her identity hidden from staff. Emotional beat: numb self-erasure, the comfort of invisibility already curdling into loneliness.

chapters.title: Static on the Evening Program
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the caretaker's flat, a radio program plays a haunting nocturne she recognizes instantly: her mother Ilse's 'Nocturne for the Postcards,' written in a notebook Tamsin still owns—never recorded, never published. It is credited to one Vivian Marsh. Emotional beat: shock breaking through protective numbness.

chapters.title: What the Notebook Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a flashback to age fourteen. She retrieves her mother's composition notebooks from storage and finds dates, marginalia, and a photograph of two women laughing on the conservatory steps—one is her mother, the other an unfamiliar woman circled in ink. Emotional beat: grief reawakened as evidence.

chapters.title: Vivian Marsh, In Print
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Research reveals Vivian Marsh is now a respected composer-in-residence at a rival institution, with three albums built on works Tamsin recognizes from Ilse's notebooks. Tamsin drafts an angry letter and burns it. Emotional beat: rage without a plan; loyalty to her mother vs. fear of exposure.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Mops Next Door
chapters.summary: Dev, a teenage student, POV. Dev notices the new janitor correcting his fingering under her breath and becomes curious about her. He leaves a sticky note on her cart: 'You know this piece better than I do.' Emotional beat: first crack in Tamsin's isolation; warmth offered by a stranger.

chapters.title: Archive Hours
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She volunteers to help the conservatory's aging archivist, Mr. Okafor, and gains access to records from her mother's teaching years. She finds a 1998 complaint filed by Ilse against a colleague—withdrawn within a week. Emotional beat: dawning suspicion that her mother fought this battle before and lost it alone.

chapters.title: The Photographs Again
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, interleaved with memory. Studying the old photographs, Tamsin realizes the woman beside her mother appears in dozens of them across a decade—the same woman, aging, always half-turned away. She learns her name from a caption: V. Marsh. Emotional beat: the stranger becomes a person; disorientation.

chapters.title: A Conversation Overheard
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev overhears two faculty dismissing rumors about Marsh's sources as 'jealous gossip from a dead woman's camp.' He tells Tamsin, not knowing why her hands shake. Emotional beat: institutional complicity revealed; Tamsin understands no one will hand her justice.

chapters.title: Withdrawn
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Through Okafor, she reads the withdrawn complaint: Ilse accused Marsh of taking manuscripts during their collaboration, but withdrew it when threatened with exposure of their relationship—and with questions about Ilse's own authorship of a piece submitted under Tamsin's childhood name. Emotional beat: shame; the past is more morally tangled than Tamsin believed.

chapters.title: The Prodigy's Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Tamsin's POV. At sixteen, Tamsin let her mother submit Tamsin's prize-winning sonata under Ilse's name to save Ilse's career, then publicly denied writing it when challenged. This denial was later used to discredit Ilse entirely. Emotional beat: guilt crystallizes—Tamsin's own lie helped bury them both.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Among Ilse's effects, Tamsin finds unsent letters to Vivian spanning twenty years—love, accusation, forgiveness attempted and revoked. The last, written weeks before Ilse's death, says only: 'Tell the truth or keep my songs; you cannot keep both.' Emotional beat: complicated love; the enemy is also a mourner.

chapters.title: Marsh Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs (Tamsin, Dev). Vivian Marsh arrives at Ashcombe for a gala honoring her 'Collected Early Works.' Tamsin, pushing a mop cart, stands ten feet from the woman in the photographs. Marsh looks at her twice, and the second time, hesitates. Emotional beat: dread and recognition; the invisible tenant is seen.

chapters.title: Ten Feet Away
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Marsh approaches her privately: 'You have her hands.' They speak in a stairwell—Marsh admits she took the manuscripts but claims Ilse gave them freely as penance for something Tamsin doesn't yet understand. Emotional beat: confrontation without resolution; every certainty wobbles.

chapters.title: Penance
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, deep flashback. Tamsin pieces together what Ilse owed: decades ago, Ilse passed off a dying friend's—Vivian's—early work as her own to win the post that made her career. The thefts ran both directions, a wound passed back and forth for thirty years. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; there is no innocent party, only damage.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev, emboldened, plans to publish an analysis online showing the stylistic fingerprints linking Marsh's albums to Ilse's notebooks. Tamsin begs him to stop—not to protect Marsh, but because she isn't ready for the scrutiny that will expose her own old lie. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made literal; Tamsin chooses silence again and hates it.

chapters.title: The Memory Going
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Visiting Ilse's former neighbor, Tamsin learns details of her mother's final year—the humiliation, the drinking, the nights she played the Nocturne to an empty room. Tamsin realizes the memory she's protecting is partly a fiction she built to survive. Emotional beat: mourning the real mother, not the monument.

chapters.title: Okafor's Box
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Okafor, retiring, gives Tamsin a box Ilse deposited with him years ago: the original dated manuscripts, correspondence proving both women's thefts, and Ilse's final unfinished piece, 'Interior for the Postcards,' with a note: 'For whoever finishes it honestly.' Emotional beat: inheritance accepted; the choice can no longer be avoided.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev publishes his analysis anyway; it spreads through the conservatory within days. Marsh faces calls to withdraw from the gala. Tamsin watches the storm she tried to contain break without her—and sees that the truth arrived crooked, missing its most important witness. Emotional beat: consequences outpacing courage; regret sharpened.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Old Photographs
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin visits Marsh on the eve of the gala. They read Ilse's letters aloud to each other, trading confessions across the table. Marsh agrees to publicly acknowledge Ilse if Tamsin will acknowledge her own role in the original betrayal. Emotional beat: forgiveness begun—not absolution, but mutual recognition.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At a conservatory arbitration panel convened over the manuscripts, Tamsin discloses everything: Ilse's theft, Marsh's theft, and her own sixteen-year-old lie. The panel is stunned; some pity her, some condemn her. She asks for neither punishment nor credit—only corrected attribution. Emotional beat: climax; truth spoken at full cost, freedom in the exposure.

chapters.title: Attribution
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The conservatory revises its archives: the works are credited jointly, with a permanent exhibit telling the whole tangle. Marsh performs the Nocturne at the rescheduled gala and names Ilse from the stage. Dev watches Tamsin in the audience, the janitor no longer hiding. Emotional beat: imperfect justice; belonging earned through honesty rather than innocence.

chapters.title: Interior for the Postcards
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the last night of term, Tamsin sits at the conservatory's neglected hall piano and finishes her mother's final piece, playing it through once, badly and completely, for an audience of one student who stays to listen. She signs the manuscript with both names—hers and her mother's. Emotional beat: resolution; the tenant becomes the owner of her own life.
